executive_summary: AUD/JPY is anchored at 112.1938, the close of 2026-09-03 in the gated price store, meaning one Australian dollar buys 112.1938 yen. The pair has gone nowhere for six months and everywhere for twelve: −0.58% over three months and −1.36% over six against +14.64% over one year, leaving spot at the 86th percentile of its 96.572–114.83705 fifty-two-week closing range and 13.41% above a 200-week average at 98.92406 that has never turned. The dominant bilateral narrative is a 335bp policy differential — the widest bilateral gap in the eleven-currency benchmark set — that is about to be compressed from one side only, because the BoJ has roughly 50–75bp of tightening left against an RBA that has one move left to a fully priced 4.60% terminal. What diverges most from the standalone dossiers is the netting: read separately, an AUD book crowded long and a JPY book at only the 33rd percentile short look like two uncrowded trades; read bilaterally they are one trade, expressed on both legs of the same 2026-08-25 CFTC report, and the bilateral energy transfer that has been paying Australia through Japan's 22.1%-of-imports fuel bill is forecast by Australia's own bank economists to peak this quarter. The settled verdict is tactically Neutral, conviction 2 (score +0.0134) and strategically Bearish, conviction 3 (score −0.3363), and the price payload corroborates the strategic call more aggressively than the tactical one: the two sessions to 2026-09-03 took the pair 1.98% lower with a 222-pip range on the final day, 2.9 times ATR(14), pushing spot below both the 50-day and 100-day averages. Post-payload reporting describes exactly the mechanism the strategic Bearish anticipated already engaging — a rush to unwind yen-funded carry trades pushed the yen to a one-month high against the dollar as traders raised bets on a larger Bank of Japan rate hike after hawkish comments from Governor Ueda, ahead of the September 18 decision — which is the report's honest caveat: the tactical Neutral was scored without a chart and may already be behind the tape, but the scored stance stands as issued and the skew is expressed through the path and the downside target rather than through the number.

market_context.valuation_assessment: At the pair level this is the largest real dislocation in the G10 and it has been for years. The BIS REER for June 2026 puts Australia at 115.92 — the highest in the eleven-currency set after a +10.36-point twelve-month real appreciation — and Japan at 65.3, the cheapest, 30.4 points below the next-cheapest currency. The base dossier scores the AUD/JPY relative real deviation at 77.5%, the largest in its table; the quote dossier's mirror construction gives −43.67% and a mechanical REER-parity cross of 64.60. Both observations are relative real-exchange-rate gaps against each index's own 2020 base period, not PPP fair values, and both are 63 days old at the valuation date, marginally outside the 60-day strategic freshness window. What is priced into 112.1938 is a differential that persists rather than a real exchange rate that mean-reverts.

bilateral_carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Spot can fall 376 pips (3.4%) over a year, 94 pips over a quarter, or 31 pips over a month before carry is erased; against ATR(14) of 78 pips one average day wipes out roughly two and a half months of carry, and the 2026-09-03 session alone erased more than seven months of it
bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The differential is 335bp — RBA cash rate 4.35% against the BoJ target of 'around 1.0 percent' — producing 376 pips of annual carry on spot 112.1938. Carry-to-vol on the store's 94.7-day estimate is 0.415, the most attractive ratio in the yen complex, though the estimate is a documented floor and the true ratio is probably closer to 0.36. The carry regime is 'working' because VIX at 14.51, tight credit spreads and strong equity performance are precisely the conditions that reward a funded long, which is why both legs were being added to through August. The regime broke once already this year when Japan spent a record roughly JPY 15.4 trillion supporting the yen between 30 July and 26 August, including a rare coordinated intervention with the United States, and reassembled inside four weeks — evidence that official flow alone does not change the regime. What changes it is a volatility event: a move in 60-day realised vol from 8.07% to the 12-15% range takes the carry-to-vol ratio from 0.415 toward 0.24 and destroys the position's risk-adjusted case without any change in rates. Forward outrights sit below spot, so by the standard covered-interest-parity reading a long AUD/JPY accrues the differential and a short pays it; the futures calendar-spread premium of -348.6bp annualised implies roughly -14bp of cross-currency basis against the 335bp interest gap.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: High-carry pair: the AUD-JPY policy differential of 335bp is the widest bilateral gap in the eleven-currency benchmark set on both dossiers' own tables, and the pair is the canonical G10 carry expression, so the rate channel carries more of the pair's variance than the default assumes.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral differential is enormous and, over four weeks, static. The RBA cash rate is 4.35% and the BoJ target is 'around 1.0 percent', a spread of 335bp. On ten-year yields the gap is 216.1bp on the cached monthly basis and 213.7bp on the live basis both dossiers quote for 2026-08-31 - essentially unchanged over three months, so the term-premium channel is not currently moving. What is genuinely in play is a pair of September binaries pointing in opposite directions: the BoJ decision on 18 September is roughly 80-90% priced for +25bp to 1.25%, while the RBA decision on 29 September is roughly 47-50% priced for +25bp to 4.60%. Probability-weighting those two gives an expected change in the differential of only about -9bp against a 335bp level, which is noise. The transmission is the carry channel: at 335bp against a store-estimated 3-month ATM implied volatility of 8.074%, the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.415, the most attractive in the yen complex, and a long AUD/JPY spot position accrues roughly 0.31 yen a month. The offsetting fact is that the futures curve already charges for it: the store's calendar-spread premium is -348.6bp annualised against a 335bp interest differential, so a rolled long position pays about 14bp a year more than the differential and receives none of the carry. Two live binaries of opposite sign plus a differential that does not move inside the window is a Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the differential stops being static and starts compressing, and it compresses from one side only. The RBA is priced to a 4.60% terminal with about 30bp of cumulative tightening to February 2027 and its own August forecasts do not return trimmed-mean inflation to the band midpoint until early 2028, so the Australian leg has roughly one move left. The BoJ leg has considerably more: half of 36 surveyed economists now name 1.75% as terminal and 36% name 2.00% or higher, and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027, against a curve that implies only about 1.21% after the 18 December decision. On those two paths the bilateral policy gap goes from 335bp today to roughly 310bp after 18 September, and toward 285-260bp through the 30 October Outlook Report and the 18 December decision - a 15-22% reduction in the single load-bearing support of a long AUD/JPY position. Note the asymmetry of delivery risk at the December RBA: a hike to 4.60% is fully priced there, so delivery is neutral for the pair and non-delivery is sharply negative, while at the BoJ the unpriced tail is a faster pace rather than a slower one. The transmission runs through both the carry level and the forward curve: as the differential compresses the forward discount widens toward the interest gap, and the pair's total-return cushion thins with it.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is wide and roughly stable while the growth differential is turning against the base currency, and the two cancel over four weeks. Australia's July headline CPI was 3.5% against a 3.2% consensus with the trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% and services accelerating from 3.5% to 3.7%. Japan's July national core was 1.8% with core-core 1.9% and the BoJ's own ex-special-factors measure 2.3%, and Tokyo core has accelerated three consecutive months. That leaves a headline gap of roughly 160bp in Australia's favour, but the gap is narrowing at the margin. On growth the direction of travel is unambiguously the other way: Australian unemployment is at a post-COVID high of 4.5% with employment down 15,800, private capex -3.6% quarter on quarter against a +0.8% consensus; Japanese unemployment fell to 2.4%, composite PMI 53.4, June Tankan +22 large manufacturers and +37 large non-manufacturers - best since 1991. Asymmetric sensitivity favours the Australian leg tactically because Australian prints feed a live 50% policy binary while Japanese prints feed an already 85%-priced one, but the Japanese 17 September CPI carries an identified upside skew inside the same window. A wide-but-narrowing inflation gap against a clearly deteriorating relative growth gap is a Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the two macro trajectories diverge in the pair's disfavour. Australia's own central bank forecasts underlying inflation falling to 3.3% by end-2026 and does not reach the band midpoint until early 2028, a grinding disinflation that removes the acceleration currently driving the base currency without removing the level; the growth side is deteriorating on every observable measure and S&P projects Australian real GDP slowing to 1.5% in fiscal 2027. Japan's path runs the other way: the BoJ's July Outlook has core CPI at 2.5% for FY2026 and 2.4% for FY2027 - the FY2027 figure revised UP - with the FY2026 cut explicitly attributed to temporary energy subsidies. Add a third consecutive shunto above 5%, six straight months of positive real wages and household inflation expectations at a record 90.4% breadth, and the Japanese inflation regime is hardening while the Australian one softens. The bilateral inflation gap therefore compresses from roughly 160bp toward 100bp or less over the horizon, the same compression Factor 1 prices in nominal rates. The counter, which caps confidence at 55, is that Japan's price breadth remains narrow - a weighted median of 1.1% and services at 1.2% against goods at 2.7% - so the acceleration is still substantially imported and would fade with energy.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor where the two dossiers reinforce each other cleanly in the same direction for the pair: the AUD dossier scores risk appetite Bullish AUD at 60 and the JPY dossier scores it Bearish JPY at 60, and for AUD/JPY those are the same call. The bilateral differential is structural rather than cyclical - Australia has the highest equity and commodity beta in the G10 and Japan supplies the funding leg with the strongest negative correlation to VIX - so the pair is the purest cross-asset expression of the risk regime, and the regime is benign. VIX closed at 14.51 on 27 August, near the 2026 low of 14.13; US investment-grade OAS is 79bp and high-yield 263bp, near historic tights; the S&P 500 is +13.1% year to date and the Nikkei +58.4% year on year. The Federal Reserve Chair has described credit spreads as near the low end of their historical ranges. Transmission is mechanical: at low realised volatility a 335bp differential is comfortable to hold. Two live qualifications hold confidence at 62 rather than higher: complacency has been named going into the historically choppy mid-August to mid-October window, and US and Iranian forces exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on 30-31 August, the specific escalation route that would flip this factor inside days.

The modal path is persistence: if VIX stays near 14 and credit near 79bp/263bp, the pair grinds higher on carry. But the distribution around that modal path is severely left-skewed for this cross specifically. Spreads and volatility sit at the tight end of their post-2020 ranges, so there is little room to tighten and unlimited room to widen; the AUD dossier documents drawdowns of 10-15% in a quarter as unremarkable, and the JPY dossier documents the August 2024 analogue in which a comparable carry configuration unwound roughly fifteen big figures in USD/JPY. Identified dated routes to a break inside the window are the 30 September US appropriations deadline, the 3 November US midterms, the unresolved Hormuz situation and a Fed tightening into a labour market that printed -23,000 payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions. A high-probability slow grind higher against a low-probability violent fall is a genuine Neutral with a fat left tail.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Speculative futures books turn over every four to eight weeks and carry no strategic signal, so the strategic read rests on structural flow, and the structural flow is asymmetric against the pair. On the quote side there is a large latent yen-buying option that appears nowhere in positioning data: Japanese life-insurer hedge ratios are at historically low levels, and raising them is simultaneously spot yen demand and basis-widening pressure. GPIF closed June with foreign equities at 25.33% against a 25% target after a +16.94% quarter, mechanically implying multi-trillion-yen foreign-asset sales, and Japanese residents sold a net JPY 1,978.4bn of foreign bonds and JPY 869.0bn of foreign equities in the week to 22 August. On the base side the structural offsets are genuine but smaller: a persistent real-money short in AUD futures of -45,427 contracts that has been wrong all year, and Australian superannuation hedge rebalancing. The specifically bilateral flow weakens at the margin as the differential compresses from 335bp toward 310bp and below. Net: the latent quote-side bid outweighs the base-side bid, and the crowded speculative long will have resolved one way or another before the horizon closes.

tactical.contrarian_case: The case against our own Bearish read is that the market has now watched the yen fail to hold a record intervention, a BoJ hike and a 30-year high in JGB yields, and has concluded that yen rallies are for selling; on that reading every dip is added to, and the AUD asset-manager short of -45,427 contracts - wrong through an 8.27% year of AUD appreciation - is the genuinely crowded position whose capitulation would squeeze the pair higher rather than lower.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Structurally the pair is short the yen in places that do not appear in futures at all: record-low life-insurer hedge ratios, Japanese retail net long foreign currency at 2.05:1, a falling yen share of allocated reserves at 5.44%, and Japan slipping to third-largest net creditor. Against that sit an Australian real-money short and mechanical superannuation hedge buying. The net structural exposure is short yen, and short-yen structure is what unwinds violently.
strategic.unwind_trigger: Hedging costs falling far enough on BoJ tightening and eventual Fed easing that Japanese lifers begin normalising hedge ratios, or a Japanese fiscal-year-end repatriation window arriving with those ratios still at record lows. Either converts a slow drift into self-reinforcing spot yen demand.
strategic.historical_analogue: The RBA's own 2009 work on Japanese retail margin accounts in AUD/JPY documents exactly this pattern - large leveraged positions held into a turn produced outsized losses when carry returns went negative in 2008 - and the pair's 2008 unwind remains the reference case for how far a both-legs-crowded long can travel when the funding currency is bought back.
strategic.contrarian_case: The contrarian strategic case is that the structural short yen is not a position but a portfolio decision: Japanese institutions have been exporting capital for decades and continued selling yen even through the July intervention, so hedge-ratio normalisation may simply not happen inside the horizon while the 335bp differential keeps paying, in which case the crowded long is validated rather than punished.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the most genuinely bilateral factor in the pair and it currently points up. Australia and Japan are direct counterparties in the energy complex: IMF DOTS shows Australian goods exports to Japan of USD 46.7bn against imports of USD 17.7bn in 2024, a net Australian surplus of USD 29.0bn. Japanese LNG averaged USD 19.0/mmbtu in July, up 10.1% month on month and roughly 75% above pre-conflict levels, with JKM up 101.9% year on year, and Newcastle thermal coal is around USD 130/t; Japan's July mineral fuel import bill was JPY 2,680.4bn, 22.1% of all imports and up 53.5% year on year on falling volumes, and its terms of trade have collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 to 81.62 in July. Australia's terms of trade fell 4.4% quarter on quarter to 111.90 - a deterioration but from a level 30 points above Japan's. Transmission is immediate and mechanical: every dollar of the energy premium is a cost to the quote economy and a receipt to the base economy. The offset is iron ore at USD 95.34/t, essentially at the floor of its annual range; and Australia's aggregate current account is at a record deficit of 3.68% of GDP against Japan's 5.04% surplus. On balance the live bilateral flow dominates over four weeks and the stance is Bullish at 58 rather than higher.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the netting inverts, for two reasons. First, the energy premium currently transferring income from Japan to Australia is explicitly forecast to peak now: Westpac has Newcastle coal easing from USD 130/t toward USD 120/t and Japanese LNG peaking at an average of USD 18.5/mmbtu in the September quarter, and Brent has already fallen 12.0% in a month. Valuation times nothing on its own, which is why confidence is 55, but a fading windfall plus a record deficit plus a decade-scale real premium is a Bearish strategic external read.

net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Japan: imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons. July mineral fuel imports were 22.1% of all imports and up 53.5% year on year on falling volumes; JKM LNG up 101.9% y/y; Newcastle coal and crude both direct cost lines. Terms of trade 81.62, down from 90.5 in Q1 2026. Marginally benefits from cheaper iron ore as a steel producer.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the framework's direction rules leg by leg. Oil up: +AUD (mild) and --JPY (strong negative) -> net BULLISH AUD/JPY. LNG/JKM up: +AUD (Australia is a major LNG exporter to Japan) and --JPY -> net BULLISH AUD/JPY, and this is the strongest single netting in the pair because the trade is bilateral, with Japan importing USD 52.9bn of Australian goods dominated by energy and bulk commodities. Coal up: +AUD and -JPY -> BULLISH AUD/JPY. Iron ore up: ++AUD and mildly negative for an importing steel producer -> BULLISH AUD/JPY; iron ore DOWN, the current state at the annual floor, is therefore BEARISH AUD/JPY. Netting the four: with energy at conflict premia and iron ore at its floor, the energy legs dominate in magnitude, so the current net is bullish the pair. On the published forecast path the energy legs fade toward Q4 while the iron ore leg stays weak or weakens further on Simandou supply, which flips the net to bearish. The pair is therefore long the energy shock and short the iron ore cycle, and those two clocks run at different speeds.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from roughly USD 90 to USD 99: Australia gains mildly on crude and materially on the coal and LNG complex; Japan's import bill rises further and terms of trade fall below 78. Net BULLISH AUD/JPY, on the order of 1.5-2.5% on historical elasticities, but partly offset if the move arrives through a risk-negative Hormuz escalation, which hits the pair through Factor 3 harder and faster than the terms-of-trade channel helps it.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent from roughly USD 90 to USD 81: Australia loses the coal and LNG windfall currently offsetting iron ore weakness, and the RBA's causal chain from oil supply to domestic inflation to policy runs in reverse; Japan gets direct relief and its terms of trade recover toward 86. Net BEARISH AUD/JPY, larger in magnitude than the up-case because it removes a base-currency policy driver as well as an export receipt.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Japanese LNG/JKM together with Newcastle thermal coal - these move along the bilateral axis, changing both economies' terms of trade in opposite directions simultaneously, which no other commodity does. Iron ore is the second driver and currently the one working against the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are communicating hawkishly, so the bilateral question is not who sounds tighter but whose guidance sits furthest ahead of its own market pricing - and that is unambiguously the quote currency. The RBA's 11 August statement retained an explicit conditional hiking sentence, but market pricing has already caught up - roughly 47-50% for 29 September and about 30bp cumulative to February 2027 - so the guidance-to-pricing gap is close to zero and can now only disappoint. The BoJ's gap is large and measurable. Its 10 August Summary of Opinions states that the pace of rate increases will be faster than market expectations; the July Outlook reframes the objective to preventing an upward deviation; Takata dissented for 1.25% at the July meeting; Deputy Governor Himino called on 27 August for raising rates in a timely manner. Against that, the curve implies only about 1.21% after the 18 December decision. Meeting sequence matters and it favours the quote leg: the BoJ decides on 18 September, eleven days before the RBA. Add unusual external pressure - the US Treasury Secretary publicly stating at the G20 on 31 August that he expects Japanese policy to lead to a stronger yen - and the tactical guidance differential is bearish for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the credibility differential compounds the pricing differential. The RBA's guidance is durable but bounded: its own published forecasts keep inflation above the midpoint until early 2028, anchoring the front end and ruling out cuts, but the terminal it is being priced to is 4.60% with no path published beyond it. The BoJ has changed its reaction function rather than its forecast: the objective is now stabilising inflation and preventing an upward deviation, the FY2027 core forecast was revised UP to 2.4%, the interim assessment of the bond-purchase plan has been abolished so balance-sheet changes now happen ad hoc, and the purchase pace steps down from JPY 2.5trn a month to JPY 2.1trn by Q1 2027. A bank that has told the market it will move faster than expected, has removed a source of scheduled predictability, and has a hawkish dissent standing at a higher rate has more capacity to surprise in the direction that compresses this differential than the RBA has to surprise the other way. The dated anchor is the BoJ's 30 October Outlook Report. The credibility caveat that holds confidence at 60 is real: the BoJ has surprised in both directions historically and the FX market has sold the yen through an entire hiking cycle, evidence it does not yet believe the terminal.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The dominant near-dated event risk in this pair is official flow, and it points one way only. Japan bought roughly JPY 27.1trn of yen in calendar 2026, including JPY 15,399.3bn between 30 July and 26 August and a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July, against a previous full-year record of JPY 15.32trn. There is a well-capitalised, publicly committed buyer of the quote currency and no corresponding official seller of, or buyer of, the base currency - Australia has no FX operation and no election before May 2028. AUD/JPY is also a favoured vehicle for the exposure intervention targets, and the pair is asymmetrically exposed to the second event cluster: FOMC 16 September, BoJ 18 September and RBA 29 September, three binaries in fourteen days. The genuinely two-sided variable is the Middle East. Escalation raises Japan's import bill, bullish through Factor 5, but is risk-negative, bearish through Factor 3, and for a pair with this beta the risk channel dominates on the day. Against the Bearish stance stands the demonstrated half-life of intervention: more than half of the July move was retraced inside four weeks, and roughly 95% of respondents to an August Reuters poll said intervention alone would not sustainably curb yen weakness.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential in this pair is the widest of any factor and it favours the base currency decisively. Australia is AAA/AAA/Aaa with all three agencies on stable outlook, S&P having affirmed in August 2026, with a 2026-27 underlying cash deficit of 1.0% of GDP - the strongest sovereign position in the eleven-currency set. Japan is A1/A+/A with general government gross debt above 200% of GDP and a record debt-service line of JPY 36.6trn built on an assumed rate raised from 3.0% to 3.8%. The bilateral transmission is subtler than the ratings gap: Japanese yields are rising partly on fiscal risk premium rather than policy expectation - the 10-year JGB touched 3.00% on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 2-year hit a 31-year high and 25s30s is INVERTED at -1.0bp - and risk-premium yield rises carry no currency-positive content. To the extent the JGB move is fiscal rather than monetary, it is quote-currency negative and therefore pair-positive. The tactical expression is a 30-year auction on 3 September after a 2-year auction drew a bid-to-cover of 2.97 against a 12-month average of 3.74. Confidence is 56 because roughly 90% of JGBs are domestically held and no agency has acted in 2026.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically this is the pair's strongest structural support and the cleanest offset to a compressing differential. The arithmetic compounds: the Japanese debt-service line rose roughly JPY 5.36trn in one budget cycle purely on an assumed-rate revision, so every 100bp the BoJ adds costs about JPY 5trn or 0.9% of GDP, and the BoJ is simultaneously reducing JGB purchases from JPY 2.5trn a month to JPY 2.1trn by Q1 2027 - supply rising as the dominant buyer withdraws. That is the specific mechanism by which the quote currency's own tightening cycle becomes quote-negative, and it is the reason the yen failed to rally through a 30-year high in JGB yields. Australia runs the mirror image: net debt rising only from 18.8% to a projected 21.9% by 2029-30 from an exceptionally low base, an AAA affirmed with a stable outlook, the highest AAA-rated 10-year yield in the developed world, and genuine fiscal space to stimulate if growth cracks. The dated catalyst is the FY2027 draft budget approval in late December. Qualifications: roughly 90% domestic JGB ownership caps rollover risk, all three agencies are on stable outlook with no 2026 action.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For a cross the USD channel is indirect, and the two dossiers happen to read it as negative for their own currency - the AUD dossier scores it Bearish AUD, the JPY dossier Bearish JPY - so the pair question is which leg loses more from a hawkish Fed running an easy plumbing. On the evidence, the funding leg does. There is no dollar funding stress anywhere: SOFR printed 3.65% against interest on reserves at 3.65%, standing repo usage was effectively nil through August, QT ended in December 2025 and the Desk is now buying bills to maintain ample reserves with the balance sheet at USD 6.73trn and reserves at USD 2.92trn. Abundant, cheap dollars with a hawkish Fed - roughly 57-66% priced for a hike on 16 September - is the classic configuration in which carry compounds smoothly, because there is no squeeze to force a funded position out. The offsets that hold confidence to 52 are real: a hawkish Fed compresses the base leg's own carry versus the dollar from 72.5bp toward 40bp, and the broad dollar has actually fallen 2.08% on the month even as the priced path turned hawkish. On the pair's own funding, the store's rolled premium of -348.6bp against a 335bp differential implies roughly 14bp of basis against the base currency - a modest structural cost, nowhere near stress.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: The strategic base case is unchanged and mildly pair-supportive: with QT over, the Desk buying bills and reserves near USD 2.92trn, dollar availability will not constrain global risk-taking inside the horizon, and the Federal Reserve Chair has explicitly demoted balance-sheet policy while saying he would be hard pressed to call financial conditions restrictive - which makes easy conditions an argument for more rate hikes rather than a limit on them. First, the yen cross-currency basis: Japan's USD 550bn US investment commitment is expected to push the five-to-ten-year dollar-yen basis more negative through receiving flows, and a life-insurer hedge-ratio normalisation would widen the short-dated basis while generating spot yen demand. Neither dossier can source a quoted three-month basis, so neither can tell how far either channel has progressed; that is the largest unresolved input on this factor.

tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights this pair is decided by three channels and they cancel. The carry channel, weighted up to 0.27 because 335bp is the widest bilateral policy gap in the set, is Neutral on purpose: the differential does not move inside four weeks, the BoJ decision on 18 September is roughly 80-90% priced and the RBA decision on 29 September roughly 47-50% priced, and probability-weighting those two gives an expected differential change of about -9bp against a 335bp level. The risk channel, weighted up to 0.14 for the market's purest risk-proxy cross, is the largest single positive: VIX at 14.51, investment-grade at 79bp, high-yield at 263bp and equities near highs are exactly the conditions in which a 0.415 carry-to-vol position is comfortable to hold, and this is the one factor where the two dossiers reinforce in the same pair direction. The flow and official channels are the largest negative: leveraged funds are long the base leg at +54,061 contracts and short the quote leg at -77,042 contracts on the same CFTC report, which for the pair is one crowded trade rather than two uncrowded ones, and the quote currency has a publicly committed two-government bid behind it after roughly JPY 27.1trn of intervention in 2026. The standalone dossiers interact in a way that matters: read naively, the base dossier's +0.2756 against the quote dossier's +0.1270 would imply a mildly bullish pair, and the quote dossier's own G10 table places the base currency above it tactically. The bilateral lens takes that away, because three of the pair-specific offsets - combined positioning, the guidance-to-pricing gap, and one-directional official flow - do not appear in either standalone score. What is priced versus what we expect: the market prices both September hikes and a benign regime, and our edge is narrow and non-directional - the pair's own estimated vol surface is in contango through a fortnight containing two central bank decisions and is a documented floor, so the September cluster is under-charged in both directions rather than mispriced in one. The path of least resistance is a two-sided grind, with the bilateral energy transfer and the fiscal quality differential supporting the pair while positioning and guidance lean on it. Dated catalysts inside the window: the 3 September Japanese 30-year auction, 4 September US payrolls and CFTC, 15 September Japanese trade statistics, 16 September FOMC, 17 September Japanese CPI, 18 September BoJ and 29 September RBA. Conviction is 2 because the score is near zero by cancellation of individually meaningful forces rather than by absence of information, and because 41% of the applied weight is deliberately parked at Neutral.

strategic.score_interpretation: -0.3363 is beyond -0.10, so the derived net stance is Bearish, and the reading is broad rather than concentrated. Six factors contribute -0.4133 and only two contribute +0.0770, with risk appetite and event risk both Neutral. The largest single contribution is policy and rates at -0.1566, which is 47% of the gross negative but only because that factor carries the heaviest weight; on a per-unit-weight basis the confidences are tightly clustered between 50 and 60, meaning no factor is doing outsized work and the result is the sum of six independently modest bearish reads. Breadth is therefore the honest description, and it cuts both ways: a score assembled from six factors at 50-60 confidence is more robust to any one factor being wrong than a score driven by a single 80-confidence call, but it is also a score with no dominant mechanism to point at. Two things temper it. First, the two positive contributions - Australia's AAA sovereign quality against a Japanese fiscal arithmetic that worsens with every BoJ hike, and an easy dollar plumbing that lets carry compound - are the pair's genuine structural supports and they are levels rather than trajectories, so they do not fade. Second, the single largest bearish mechanism, differential compression, has repeatedly failed to move spot this year, which the quote dossier itself calls its central puzzle.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the pair loses on breadth. Policy and rates at 0.27 turns Bearish because the differential compresses from one side only: the base leg is priced to a 4.60% terminal with roughly one move left and its own central bank does not see the band midpoint until 2028, while the quote leg faces an economist distribution centred on a 1.75% terminal against a curve implying barely 1.21% after 18 December - a path that takes 335bp toward 285-260bp by Q1 2027. External balance at 0.16 turns Bearish because the commodity netting inverts on its own forecast path: the coal and LNG premium currently transferring income along a USD 29bn bilateral trade axis is forecast to peak this quarter, and what remains is an Australian record current-account deficit of 3.68% of GDP against a Japanese 5.04% surplus and the largest real exchange-rate gap in the G10, with BIS REERs of 115.92 and 65.3. Guidance at 0.12 is Bearish because only one of the two banks has told the market it intends to move faster than the market expects. The two dossiers now conflict where they previously agreed: the base dossier is strategically Neutral at +0.0670 and ranks itself 5th of 11, while the quote dossier is strategically Bullish at +0.0940 and ranks itself 3rd, explicitly above the base currency - so the cross-sectional read from the inputs themselves points the same way as this bilateral score. The bilateral factors that modify the standalone views are the ones that matter most here: the both-legs-crowded speculative long, the latent Japanese repatriation and hedge-ratio option that appears in no positioning series, and the fiscal insight that runs the other way - that part of the JGB yield rise is risk premium, not policy, which makes the quote currency's own tightening cycle self-limiting and is the pair's best structural defence. What is priced versus what we expect: an aggregator consensus path already has the pair softer through 2027, so direction is not the disagreement; the disagreement is that the market's own instruments price an orderly path, with a pair vol surface in contango, a decaying long-dated yen skew, and a rolled futures premium that charges more than the differential. The path of least resistance is a grinding decline punctuated by carry-funded rallies, because the pair needs continuous positive news simply to hold a 335bp funded long while the negative catalysts are scheduled. Those catalysts are dated: the Australian Q3 CPI in late October, the BoJ Outlook Report on 30 October, the RBA on 3 November, then the RBA on 8 December, the BoJ on 18 December and the Japanese FY2027 budget round. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the dominant mechanism has demonstrably failed to move spot all year and because two of the three bearish heavyweights depend on variables we cannot forecast - the oil price and Chinese steel demand.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically this ranks as the least attractive long and among the more attractive shorts in the AUD complex: the base dossier's own relative-value work names AUD/JPY the cleanest bullish AUD expression on carry while conceding the entry is the worst available in twelve months, and the quote dossier names AUD/JPY its cleanest bearish-yen expression, which is the same statement viewed from the other side. Against AUD/CHF, the franc leg has no compression pathway at all while the yen leg has 50-75bp of tightening still to deliver, so AUD/CHF is the better structural carry and AUD/JPY the better short. Against AUD/NZD and AUD/NOK, both express policy convergence at a fraction of the carry cost. Among yen crosses, short AUD/JPY carries the highest cost but also the highest convexity to a regime break, which is why the quote dossier ranks it first as a risk hedge rather than as a directional trade.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge and the divergence is produced almost entirely by two factors changing stance as their weights change. Policy and rates carries 0.27 on both horizons but flips from Neutral to Bearish, worth -0.1566, because a differential that cannot move in four weeks compresses by 50-75bp on the published paths over one to three months. External balance carries 0.06 tactically and 0.16 strategically and flips from Bullish to Bearish, worth -0.1228 of swing, because the energy premium that currently transfers income along the bilateral axis is forecast to peak this quarter. Those two alone account for -0.279 of the -0.350 difference between the scores. Risk appetite adds the rest by moving from Bullish to Neutral as a level signal becomes a distribution signal.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Late October to early November 2026: the Australian Q3 CPI in the last week of October, followed by the BoJ decision with its Outlook Report on 2026-10-30 - the only projection round flagged in the gated calendar for either currency in this window - and the RBA decision on 2026-11-03. The Australian print resolves whether the July inflation acceleration was signal or noise; the Japanese projection round resolves whether the terminal moves toward 1.75%. Both land inside five days.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The two horizons are not in conflict about the world, only about the clock: the tactical Neutral says a 335bp funded long is comfortable while the regime holds and nothing is scheduled to break it, and the strategic Bearish says the things scheduled to break it are dated. The practical implication is that any long expression is a defined-horizon carry trade that should be re-underwritten before the 30 October Outlook Report rather than rolled through it, and that the strategic view is expressed better against the funding cost than with it - the rolled futures premium of -348.6bp charges more than the 335bp differential, so a short is paid marginally more than the interest gap to wait while a long receives none of it in the roll.

catalysts.rationale: The most important Japanese activity indicator and, for this pair, the one that updates the corporate exchange-rate planning assumption that drives hedging flow. The June survey had large non-manufacturers at +37, the best since 1991, and capex plans revised up 7.2 points. A repeat hardens the quote-currency policy path exactly as the base currency's own surveys deteriorate, which is the Factor 2 strategic crossing.

Australia publishes headline and trimmed-mean CPI quarterly, so three months of expectations compress into one number and the base leg reacts violently. This release resolves the central market disagreement - whether the July acceleration was signal or noise - and therefore whether the base leg has one more hike or none. It is the resolution event for the tactical carry cushion.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: Gated calendar, firm, and the only projection round flagged for either currency in the window - a projection meeting moves a pair materially harder than a bare statement. Consensus locates the next hike here or in December, taking the differential from 310bp toward 285bp, and the accompanying forecast revisions are how this central bank signals its path. The July Outlook already revised FY2027 core up to 2.4% and describes CPI risks as skewed to the upside.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board decision
catalysts.rationale: Gated calendar, firm. Four of the Big Four houses locate the hike to 4.60% here, and the base dossier reports that the quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy accompanies it. Delivery plus an upward forecast revision would open a 4.85% path and is pair-positive; a downward revision closes the base leg's cycle and is pair-negative. It is the tactical-to-strategic handover for the pair.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia Monetary Policy Board decision
catalysts.rationale: Gated calendar, firm. A hike to 4.60% by December is fully priced, which makes this the most asymmetric base-leg event in the window: delivery is neutral for the pair and non-delivery removes roughly 25bp of priced differential in one session. It also sits ten days before the BoJ decision, so the December sequence runs base leg first for the only time in the window.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: Gated calendar, firm, and the largest single gap between guidance and pricing in either dossier: the curve implies roughly 1.21% after this meeting against a Board that has said the pace will be faster than the market expects and an economist distribution centred on a 1.75% terminal. A move here would be a repricing rather than a confirmation, and it compresses the pair's differential toward 285bp with the base leg already at its priced terminal.

Moving averages, zones, 52-week statistics and 200-week figures are computed over the whole stored history (2007-12-24 to 2026-09-03, 4,878 weekday bars), not over the 130 bars shown.

Only 1 resistance zone against 9 support zones met the 2-touch threshold in the payload's own data-quality note; the resistance table is supplemented with the 52-week highs, the 50-day and 100-day averages, and round numbers, each labelled as a supplement rather than a computed zone.

spotDate 2026-09-03 is two days after the 2026-09-01 valuation date, an unusual direction of gap. Both dossiers were written to a 2026-08-28 AUD/JPY cross of 114.669; every level, target and distance in this report is computed against 112.1938 for internal consistency, and the 2.475-yen difference from the dossiers' cross is disclosed without fundamental inference drawn from it. The payload spot was not replaced with a fresher web quote despite post-payload reporting of further yen strength, because substituting spot while leaving averages and zone distances on the stored series would make every stated distance wrong.

Implied volatility is an estimate and a documented floor: the payload's impliedVol block is flagged estimate:true, built by a triangle realised-correlation method with implied correlation 0.4324 because AUD/JPY has no listed option; the method runs 8.7-17.8% low against direct quotes and 14.4% low at the median across seventeen pairs.

Forward outrights are derived from the payload's funding.premiumBp of -348.6bp annualised (cme_calendar_spread_cross method), applied actual/365; these are model forwards from a listed-futures calendar spread, not dealer quotes, and by covered interest parity the premium is the interest differential plus roughly -14bp of cross-currency basis, not decomposable further without an OIS curve.

Convention note disclosed: forward outrights sit below spot, so on the standard covered-interest-parity reading a long AUD/JPY accrues and a short pays; the carried Factor 1 tactical text and the carried cross-horizon trading implication characterise the roll in the opposite sense. The standard reading is used consistently in the Bilateral Carry Analysis, Forward vs Spot and Risk/Reward sections, and the discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved by editing a carried factor.

Both ten-year yields in the payload are monthly observations as of 2026-06-01 (AUD 4.831%, JPY 2.670%) and are never quoted as live levels; where a live comparison is made, both legs use the dossiers' 2026-08-31 prints of 5.08% and 2.943%, and monthly and live bases are never mixed inside one spread.

The direction verdict (factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, contributions, net scores, conviction levels, rationales, contrarian and commodity-netting analyses, expression assessment, cross-horizon explanation and catalyst list) is reproduced verbatim from the first-pass verdict, scored without the price payload, precisely so a stance could not be reverse-engineered from a chart. No factor was re-scored based on the second-pass price data; disagreements between the scored verdict and the price payload are published as second-pass annotations rather than resolved by re-scoring.

Web research was used only for pair-specific forecast paths, named chart patterns requiring visual identification, bilateral positioning/flow commentary, and intervention/barrier context; it was not used for spot, performance, moving averages, realised volatility or support/resistance levels, all of which come from the gated store.

The only continuously updated AUD/JPY forecast path available is an aggregator blending investment-bank and technical-desk contributions into a weighted quarterly consensus with an indicative ±1% band, not a bank research survey; no single-desk AUD/JPY target could be sourced, and algorithmic/extrapolation forecast sites returned by search were excluded as a category error.

Documented conflicts flagged but not resolved: (1) China August manufacturing PMI - official NBS 49.8 vs private survey 51.5; (2) aggregate short-yen positioning - third-party estimate ~124,575 contracts vs CFTC leveraged-fund reading of -77,042; (3) Brent quoted USD 90.5-93.0 on 2026-08-31 vs cached USD 88.24 for 2026-08-25; (4) several dossier-level fiscal, ratings and tariff figures flagged as best-available or unresolved in their source documents and carried with those flags intact; (5) both dossiers' BIS REER observations are 63 days old, marginally outside the 60-day strategic freshness window, and are relative real-exchange-rate gaps rather than PPP fair values.

Bilateral trade figures are taken verbatim from the supplied IMF DOTS 2024 block and not re-estimated; the two reporting directions do not reconcile exactly (Australian exports USD 46.7bn vs Japanese imports USD 52.9bn), which is normal partner-reporting asymmetry from valuation, freight and re-export treatment.
